title: Google's Xreal Aura Ships at $1,279, Months Ahead of Meta's VR Glasses
excerpt: Xreal's Android XR glasses, developed with Google, are on pre-order in the US at $1,279 and ship before the end of 2026 — undercutting Meta's $1,299.99 VR Glasses, which don't arrive until spring 2027.
body:
• Xreal Aura is on pre-order in the US at $1,279 for the base model (12GB RAM, 256GB storage); a $1,499 top configuration offers 16GB RAM and 512GB.
  • The glasses ship in fall 2026 across the US, Canada, Japan and South Korea — roughly six months before Meta's VR Glasses launch in spring 2027 at $1,299.99.
  • Both devices run on Qualcomm's Snapdragon Reality Elite chip but take opposite display approaches: the Aura is optical see-through AR, while Meta's headset is opaque video see-through VR.
  • No India pricing or launch date has been announced for either device; the Aura's first wave covers four markets, and Samsung's Galaxy XR headset remains US-only.

The first serious price-and-release fight of the Android XR era is on. Xreal has opened pre-orders for its Aura smart glasses — developed in collaboration with Google and running Android XR — at $1,279 for the base configuration, with shipping promised before the end of 2026. That puts the device on shelves roughly six months before Meta's competing VR Glasses, announced at Meta Connect 2026 at $1,299.99 for a spring 2027 launch. The price gap is just $20. The timing gap is the story.

Two devices, one chip, opposite philosophies

Under the hood, the rivals are closer than their marketing suggests. Both devices are built around Qualcomm's Snapdragon Reality Elite platform, which Qualcomm positioned as the silicon for exactly this category: high-performance video-see-through headsets and lightweight tethered optical-see-through glasses. Xreal and Meta took the fork in different directions.

https://x.com/Gadget_Ry/status/2107806510982345007

The Aura is an optical see-through device — the wearer looks through transparent lenses at the real world, with digital content overlaid. Xreal is using Sony micro-OLED panels at 1,920 x 1,200 pixels, a 120Hz refresh rate and 1,050 nits of brightness, with a 70-degree field of view. Despite the displays, the frames weigh about 95 grams. To keep them that light, the mainboard and a 34.8Wh battery live in a separate puck connected by cable, with a fingerprint sensor, Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.3, GPS and four microphones built in. Tested units can position up to five virtual monitors freely in a room, controlled by voice or hand tracking.

Meta's VR Glasses, by contrast, are opaque: cameras rebuild the room on internal screens in full-color passthrough. The glasses and an external compute puck sit in a magnesium alloy frame at around 100 grams. Meta is leaning on its content advantage — the device is billed as the first IMAX Enhanced-certified VR device, with Disney+ VR content and the full Quest game library available on day one. Reviewers who tried both headsets ahead of the announcements report that the experiences diverge sharply precisely because of that single design choice: seeing the world through glass versus through a camera feed.

Google's Android playbook, strapped to your face

The Aura is the second major Android XR device after Samsung's Galaxy XR headset, which launched in late 2025 at $1,799 and is still only available in the US. The strategy is familiar: Google supplies the operating system and the Gemini AI integration, hardware partners build the showcase, and the ecosystem is open to other manufacturers. Samsung's own Gemini-powered AI glasses are expected as early as November, according to Korean press reports, and Google has confirmed audio-first glasses co-developed with Warby Parker and Gentle Monster for 2026, plus the more advanced tethered Project Aura with Xreal.

At least five Android XR devices are expected in 2026. Non-display audio glasses should land near Meta's Ray-Ban tier, roughly $300 to $500 — while the Aura and Meta's VR Glasses occupy the premium tier above $1,200.

What it means for Indian buyers

For now, this is a fight happening everywhere except India. Neither Xreal nor Meta has announced Indian pricing or a launch date; the Aura's first wave covers the US, Canada, Japan and South Korea, and Samsung's Galaxy XR headset never left the US. Indian tech enthusiasts will likely do what they did with the Apple Vision Pro: import, or wait.

The diaspora angle is more immediate: Indian-origin engineers are heavily represented across Google's Android XR group, Qualcomm's XR silicon teams and Meta's Reality Labs. For Indian professionals in the US, the Aura is buyable this holiday season; for everyone else, 2026 is a waiting game.

What's next

The calendar now favors Google's camp. Samsung's AI glasses are tipped for November, the Aura ships before year-end, and the Warby Parker and Gentle Monster models follow in 2026. Meta's answer — its VR Glasses at $1,299.99 — doesn't land until spring 2027, and its Orion-class true AR glasses remain a prototype. The holiday season will be the first real test of whether consumers want optical AR or camera-based VR at $1,300 — and whether a six-month head start beats a $20 discount.
